explain.say: Have you ever stared at your homework, tidied your pencils, got a snack, and still not started? Everyone does this! Motivation, which means the push to do something, often comes after you start, not before. Look at the plan: step one, pick one small step.

faq.q: How do I start when a task feels too big?
faq.a: Break it into tiny steps and do only the first one, like "write the title" or "read one page". Small steps feel easy, and each one builds momentum.
asks: My homework feels too big, what do I do?

faq.a: You promise yourself to work on something for just five minutes, and then you are allowed to stop. Most of the time, once you have started, you keep going.
asks: How does the five-minute trick work?

faq.q: Why does finishing a task feel so good?
faq.a: When you finish something, your brain releases dopamine, a feel-good chemical linked to rewards. That good feeling makes you want to do it again.
asks: Why do I like ticking things off?

faq.q: Why do I keep putting things off?
faq.a: Putting things off, called procrastination, is usually about avoiding an uncomfortable feeling, like boredom or fear of getting it wrong. It does not mean you are lazy.
asks: Am I lazy if I procrastinate?

faq.q: What if I never feel motivated about anything?
faq.a: If you have lost interest in things you used to enjoy for weeks, or feel low most days, talk to a trusted grown-up, a school counsellor or a doctor. They can help.
asks: I do not want to do anything anymore

facts: In 1927, psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik found that people remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones; this is called the Zeigarnik effect.
The Pomodoro Technique of short, timed work bursts was invented by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s and named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.
